Exoduster Thread
By 1877, Reconstruction had formally ended — the last federal troops withdrew from the South, and the political protections Black Southerners had gained after the Civil War collapsed rapidly. Black Codes, voter intimidation, and escalating violence took their place, while sharecropping trapped many families in cycles of debt with no real path to independence. Beginning in 1879, tens of thousands of Black Southerners responded by migrating to Kansas, a free state tied to the legacy of abolitionist John Brown. The movement became known as the Kansas Exodus, and its participants as "Exodusters" — a name deliberately invoking the biblical Exodus, an escape from bondage toward a promised land. Organizers like Benjamin "Pap" Singleton had quietly been building toward this moment since 1869, a full decade before it became national news.
Document 1 — "Ho for Kansas!" Broadside (1878)
Benjamin "Pap" Singleton, broadside, Nashville, TN, March 18, 1878. Kansas Historical Society.
In 1877, the last federal troops withdrew from the South, ending Reconstruction. Within a year, Singleton — a formerly enslaved Tennessean — was circulating broadsides like this one, organizing what would become a mass migration.
Kansas Historical Society

Document 4 — What Happened to Nicodemus, Kansas
Synthesized from the National Park Service, BlackPast, and the Kansas Historical Society.
Nicodemus, founded in 1877 by Black settlers recruited from Kentucky, is one of the best-documented outcomes of the Kansas Exodus.
Nicodemus survived a brutal first winter partly because of food and firewood provided by the neighboring Osage Nation. By 1886, it had become genuinely self-sufficient: Black-owned farms, two newspapers, a bank, a schoolhouse, three churches, and a general store.

But the town's fate was ultimately decided by something its residents couldn't control. In the late 1880s, three separate railroad companies all chose to bypass Nicodemus for the nearby town of Bogue instead — and the growth its founders had built toward never arrived. The population shrank for over a century afterward. Today only a few dozen residents remain, and in 1996 Congress designated Nicodemus a National Historic Site — the only Reconstruction-era, Black-founded western town still standing.

i
Nicodemus, Kansas — Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS), Library of Congress

Chinese Laborer Thread
At the same time, a very different kind of migration was underway — one actively recruited rather than self-organized. Many Chinese immigrants came from Guangdong province, a region strained by poverty and the aftermath of the Taiping Rebellion, one of the deadliest conflicts in world history; some had arrived earlier chasing the California Gold Rush. By the mid-1860s, the Central Pacific Railroad faced a severe labor shortage — white workers kept quitting for the mines — and began recruiting Chinese laborers at massive scale to blast tunnels and lay track through the Sierra Nevada. By 1868, Chinese workers made up roughly 80–90% of the Central Pacific's entire workforce, doing some of the most dangerous work on the line — work that, as today's documents show, was unevenly rewarded.
Document 5 — CPRR Recruitment, the Distance, & "The Chinese Question" Cartoon
Eleven years before the Chinese Exclusion Act (a law passed in 1882 banning most Chinese immigration — you’ll examine it directly in Document 7), this cartoon shows the debate over Chinese immigration was not one-sided.
Source A: Background — How the CPRR Recruited Workers
Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project, Stanford University; Daily Alta California, Oct. 31, 1867.
By 1865, the Central Pacific Railroad faced a severe labor shortage — white workers often quit within weeks to try their luck in the gold and silver mines. Central Pacific track boss Charles Crocker began hiring Chinese laborers, recruiting through labor contractors and word of mouth back to villages in Guangdong province, promising steady wages the railroad itself set.

By October 1867, roughly 8,000 of the 50,000 Chinese immigrants then living in California were employed on the Pacific Railroad. By 1868, Chinese workers made up roughly 80–90% of the Central Pacific's entire workforce.
Guangdong Province, China, to the Sierra Nevada — roughly 6,900 miles

Document 6 — The 1867 Strike
Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project (Stanford University); San Francisco Dispatch, July 1, 1867; Sacramento Union.
By 1867, Chinese workers had built most of the Central Pacific's route through the Sierra Nevada — and had seen firsthand how unequally they were being paid and treated.
In late June 1867, thousands of Chinese workers went on strike along the Sierra Nevada route. Their demands: pay equal to white workers (who earned about $40 a month, versus roughly $31–35 for Chinese workers), a 10-hour day for surface work and 8 hours for tunneling instead of the standard 11–12 hour day, and an end to the practice of whipping or restraining workers who tried to leave for other jobs. Unlike white workers, Chinese laborers also paid for their own food, lodging, and tools out of their wages.

The strike was peaceful and highly organized. The Central Pacific's response was to cut off the food supply to the mountain work camps. Within about a week, with no other source of food, the strikers went back to work. The company made no formal concessions.

Document 7 — Chinese Exclusion Act (May 6, 1882) & Meanwhile in California
"An Act to Execute Certain Treaty Stipulations Relating to Chinese," 47th Congress, Session I, approved May 6, 1882.
Passed just 15 years after the 1867 strike, and roughly a decade after Chinese labor finished the transcontinental railroad.
"Whereas, in the opinion of the Government of the United States the coming of Chinese laborers to this country endangers the good order of certain localities within the territory thereof: Therefore, Be it enacted... That from and after the expiration of ninety days next after the passage of this act, and until the expiration of ten years next after the passage of this act, the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended."

(A later section of this same law barred Chinese immigrants already living in the U.S. from ever becoming naturalized citizens.)
